message.content:
You are reverse-engineering a C++ URL parser library **purely as a black box**.

The only artifact is the compiled binary: /workspace/dataset/test18_executable
There is NO library source available anywhere on disk (do not go looking for url_parser.h/.cpp — it does not exist). Do not try to disassemble or run 'strings'. Use ONLY behavioral probing: run the binary with argument values and observe stdout.

Usage: /workspace/dataset/test18_executable "<url>"
With fewer than 2 argv entries it returns exit code 1 and prints nothing.

It prints EXACTLY 18 lines, in this order (one per line, via std::cout << x << std::endl):
 1  scheme()          (string)
 2  authority()       (string)
 3  userinfo()        (string)
 4  host()            (string)
 5  port()            (int, prints -1 when absent)
 6  path()            (string)
 7  query()           (string)
 8  fragment()        (string)
 9  has_scheme()      (bool printed as 1/0)
10  has_authority()
11  has_userinfo()
12  has_host()
13  has_port()
14  has_path()
15  has_query()
16  has_fragment()
17  to_string()       (string)
18  is_valid()        (bool 1/0)

A labeled probe helper already exists at /tmp/probe.sh (takes any number of url args). If missing, recreate it:

  cat > /tmp/probe.sh << 'EOS'
  #!/bin/bash
  LABELS=(scheme authority userinfo host port path query fragment has_scheme has_authority has_userinfo has_host has_port has_path has_query has_fragment to_string is_valid)
  for arg in "$@"; do
    echo "=== INPUT: [$arg]"
    mapfile -t out < <(/workspace/dataset/test18_executable "$arg"; echo "EXIT:$?")
    for i in "${!LABELS[@]}"; do printf "  %-14s [%s]\n" "${LABELS[$i]}" "${out[$i]}"; done
  done
  EOS
  chmod +x /tmp/probe.sh

Note: /tmp/probe.sh renders empty fields as []. For inputs containing characters bash would mangle, invoke the binary directly with careful quoting, or use printf/hexdump to inspect raw bytes:
  /workspace/dataset/test18_executable "$URL" | od -c | head -40

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verified; you may re-verify but do not spend most of your budget here):
- A scheme is recognized ONLY when the literal "://" appears. "mailto:user@example.com" yields NO scheme and the entire input becomes path. "//example.com/path" yields no scheme and the whole thing is path (authority is parsed only when "://" was found).
- scheme() is LOWERCASED ("HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM" -> scheme "http"), but host() case is preserved ("EXAMPLE.COM").
- authority() is RECONSTRUCTED from userinfo/host/port, not the raw substring: "http://example.com:80abc" -> authority "example.com:80"; "http://example.com:" -> authority "example.com".
- port parsing behaves like std::stoi + a range check: "80abc"->80, "+80"->80, " 80"->80, "065"->65, "0"->0, but "-80"->absent, "65536"->absent, "2147483648"->absent, "abc"->absent, ""->absent. Absent port prints -1 with has_port 0 and is omitted from authority()/to_string().
- Splitting after authority: the FIRST '#' splits off fragment (so "#a#b" -> fragment "a#b"); then within the part BEFORE that '#', the FIRST '?' splits off query. "/p#a?b" -> fragment "a?b", no query.
- has_*() appear to be "field is non-empty" for strings ("http://example.com/#" -> fragment "" and has_fragment 0), and has_port() is port != -1. BUT has_authority() is NOT simply "authority string non-empty": "http://:8080" gives authority ":8080" yet has_authority 0 (host is empty there) — pin down the real rule.
- No path normalization ("/a/./b/../c" preserved), no percent-decoding ("%7E" preserved).
- is_valid(): "" -> 0, "http://" -> 0, "http://:8080" -> 0, but "example.com" -> 1, "/just/a/path" -> 1, "mailto:user@example.com" -> 1.

YOUR JOB: exhaustively probe your assigned family below. Run MANY probes (dozens — at least 40 distinct inputs; more is better). For every behavior you claim, you MUST have run the exact input. Derive precise, implementable rules (as if writing pseudocode), and explicitly flag anything ambiguous or surprising.

Return findings as structured output. Rules must be stated so a programmer can implement them without further probing. Include the concrete probe evidence (input -> the specific field values that matter) for each rule. Prefer many small precise rules over few vague ones.

YOUR ASSIGNED FAMILY:
SCHEME DETECTION AND VALIDATION.
How is the scheme found and validated? Probe: is it the FIRST "://" or some other occurrence ("http://a://b", "a://b://c")? Does anything before "://" get accepted as a scheme, or is there a charset check (letters/digits/+/-/.)? What about "1http://x", "ht tp://x", "ht_tp://x", "h+t-t.p://x", "-a://x", "+a://x", ".a://x", "HTTP://x", "HtTp://x", "://x" (empty scheme), ":///x", "http:////x"? What if "://" appears AFTER a '?' or '#' (e.g. "/path?x=http://y", "#f://g", "path#a://b") — is the scheme still taken from it, or does query/fragment splitting happen first? What about "http:/x" and "http:x" (single slash / no slashes)? Does an invalid scheme make the whole string a path, or produce an empty scheme with authority still parsed? Determine the exact precedence between scheme detection and query/fragment splitting, since that is critical. Also check scheme with trailing/leading spaces (" http://x", "http ://x").

rules.rule: The scheme delimiter is the literal 3-byte sequence "://". A scheme/authority split is attempted ONLY if that exact substring occurs; a bare ':' with one slash or no slash never triggers it. Evidence: "http:/x" and "http:x" and "a:/:/x" all yield scheme "", has_scheme 0, and the ENTIRE input as path().

There is NO character-set validation of the scheme at all. Every byte before the delimiter is accepted verbatim, including '/', ':', '@', '\\', '%', space, tab, newline, digits, leading '+', '-', '.', and non-ASCII UTF-8 bytes. Confirmed schemes: "a/b" (a/b://c), "///" (///://x), "/" (/://x), "a:b:c" (a:b:c://d), "a::" (a::://b), "1http", "ht_tp", "ht tp", "ht\ttp", "a\\b", "a@b", "a%20b", "-a", "+a", ".a", "0", "h+t-t.p", "ÄÖÜ". None of these are rejected or downgraded to path.

The ONLY thing that suppresses scheme recognition (besides the delimiter being absent) is a '?' or '#' occurring earlier in the input than the first "://". Implement as: split fragment off at the FIRST '#' of the whole input; then split query off at the FIRST '?' of the pre-fragment part; then search for "://" only in the remaining leading segment. Evidence: "ht?tp://x" -> no scheme, path "ht", query "tp://x"; "ht#tp://x" -> no scheme, path "ht", fragment "tp://x"; "?://x" -> query "://x"; "#://x" -> fragment "://x"; "a?b#c://d" -> path "a", query "b", fragment "c://d"; "a#b?c://d" -> path "a", no query, fragment "b?c://d".

When "://" does occur before any '?' or '#', the FIRST occurrence wins; later occurrences are ordinary text. Evidence: "http://a://b" -> scheme "http", host "a", path "//b"; "a://b://c://d" -> scheme "a", host "b", path "//c://d"; "AB://CD://EF" -> scheme "ab", host "CD", path "//EF".

The search is a plain substring find, so overlapping colons shift the split: in "a:://b" the first "://" starts at index 2, giving scheme "a:" and host "b". In "a:://:b" scheme is "a:" and the remainder ":b" is the authority (empty host, port "b" unparseable -> absent).

scheme() is lowercased byte-by-byte with ASCII tolower only: 'A'-'Z' -> 'a'-'z', every other byte (including UTF-8 continuation/high bytes) is left untouched. Evidence: "HTTPÄ://x" -> scheme bytes h t t p 0xC3 0x84 (verified with od -c); "HtTp://x" -> "http"; "A+B-C.D://x" -> "a+b-c.d". Host, path, query and fragment keep their original case ("Http://EXAMPLE.com/PaTh?QuEry#FrAg" -> host "EXAMPLE.com", path "/PaTh", query "QuEry", fragment "FrAg").

An input beginning with "://" yields an EMPTY scheme (has_scheme 0) but the authority IS still parsed from the text after the delimiter. Evidence: "://x" -> scheme "", has_scheme 0, authority "x", host "x", has_authority 1, has_host 1; "://u@h:1/p?q#f" -> userinfo "u", host "h", port 1, path "/p", query "q", fragment "f", has_scheme 0.

to_string() emits the "scheme://" + authority() prefix ONLY when has_scheme() is true. If the scheme is empty but an authority was parsed, the authority (and userinfo/host/port) is silently DROPPED from to_string(), making it lossy. Evidence: "://x" -> to_string "" (verified byte-exact empty line via od); "://x:80" -> ""; "://u@h:1/p?q#f" -> "/p?q#f"; "://a?b://c" -> "?b://c"; "://a/b?c#d" -> "/b?c#d".

Full to_string() formula consistent with every probe: (has_scheme() ? scheme() + "://" + authority() : "") + path() + (has_query() ? "?" + query() : "") + (has_fragment() ? "#" + fragment() : ""). Note authority() is the RECONSTRUCTED string and is emitted even when has_authority() is 0. Evidence: "http:////x" -> "http://"+""+"//x" = "http:////x"; "a:://:b" -> "a:"+"://"+""+"" = "a:://"; "http://:8080" -> "http://:8080" (authority ":8080" though has_authority 0); "a://?" -> "a://" (empty query delimiter dropped).

After a recognized "://", the authority runs to the first '/' in the remaining (already query/fragment-stripped) segment; that '/' and everything after it is the path. If the delimiter is immediately followed by '/', the authority is empty. Evidence: "a:///b" -> scheme a, authority "", has_authority 0, path "/b"; "http:////x" -> path "//x"; "a://///b" -> path "///b"; ":///x" -> no scheme, no authority, path "/x", to_string "/x".

Because query/fragment are split before authority parsing, '?' and '#' also terminate the authority. Evidence: "http://a#b:80" -> host "a", port -1, fragment "b:80" (NOT host "a#b" port 80); "http://a#b/c" -> host "a", path "", fragment "b/c"; "http://a?b/c" -> host "a", path "", query "b/c"; "http://a:8#0" -> port 8, fragment "0".

No whitespace is ever trimmed, at any position. Leading/trailing spaces become part of the scheme and are reproduced by to_string(). Evidence: " http://x" -> scheme " http", to_string " http://x"; "http ://x" -> scheme "http "; "a  ://x" -> scheme "a  "; " ://x" -> scheme " " (has_scheme 1!); "  ://x" -> scheme "  "; "\t://x" -> scheme "\t"; "s:// ?q" -> host " ", has_host 1, is_valid 1.

has_scheme() is exactly scheme().empty() == false. The only way to get an empty-but-present delimiter is the input starting with "://" (or the pre-query segment starting with it). A whitespace-only scheme still sets has_scheme 1.

An 'invalid-looking' scheme never causes a fallback re-parse: there is no code path that turns a bad scheme into a path. Either "://" is found in the leading segment (scheme + authority parsed, whatever the scheme text) or it is not (whole leading segment becomes path). Evidence: "a/b://c" keeps scheme "a/b" with host "c" and path ""; "a%3A%2F%2Fb" (percent-encoded) -> no scheme, path is the whole string (no percent-decoding before the search).
No length limit on the scheme was found: a 300-character 'A' run before "://" produced a 300-character lowercased scheme and round-tripped through to_string().

Side observation from these probes: is_valid() == (has_host() || has_path()). Scheme presence is irrelevant to validity. Evidence: "a://" -> 0; "abc://" -> 0; "://:8080" -> 0 (port only); "?://x" -> 0 (query only); "#://x" -> 0 (fragment only); "http://?q" -> 0; "://x" -> 1 (host only); ":///x" -> 1 (path only); "s:// ?q" -> 1 (host is a single space).

A newline inside argv ends up inside the scheme, so the program then prints MORE than 18 physical lines (the scheme field itself spans two lines). Evidence: $'ht
tp://x' -> scheme "ht
tp". Any consumer that assumes exactly 18 lines must treat fields as 
-delimited-with-embedded-newlines only if it knows the input.

evidence.note: FIRST :// wins; second :// stays in path; to_string reconstructs authority so raw 'a:' becomes 'a'

ASCII-only tolower; 0xC3 0x84 bytes unchanged (od -c verified)

host is a single space, counts as present and makes is_valid 1

ambiguities: Two formulations are behaviorally IDENTICAL across all 125 probes and I could not construct a discriminating input: (A) split fragment at first '#', then query at first '?' of the remainder, then look for "://" in what is left; (B) find the first "://" in the whole string and reject the scheme if a '?' or '#' occurs before it, then split. Implement either; (A) is simpler and also explains why '?' and '#' terminate the authority.

Relatedly, I cannot tell whether authority parsing stops at '/', '?', '#' natively or only at '/' because '?'/'#' were already stripped. "http://a#b:80" (host "a", fragment "b:80") is consistent with both.

to_string() dropping the whole authority when the scheme is empty ("://u@h:1/p?q#f" -> "/p?q#f") is surprising and lossy. It is consistent with 'authority is only concatenated inside the has_scheme branch', but I cannot rule out a different internal shape that happens to agree on every probe.
No upper bound on scheme length was found (tested 300 chars). A limit above 300 cannot be excluded.
Case folding was only observed under the default C locale. tolower() behaviour under other locales (e.g. Turkish dotless i) is untestable through argv alone; bytes >= 0x80 were left unchanged here.
A newline inside the scheme makes the program emit more than 18 physical lines, so 'exactly 18 lines' is not strictly true for inputs containing '\n'.

Whether an empty scheme (input starting with "://") is stored as an empty string with a separate 'found' flag, or whether has_scheme is derived purely from emptiness, cannot be distinguished; both predict identical output for every probe I ran.
